 Health Follow Unfollow Recent posts Alabama Arise warns proposed SNAP rule could increase hunger
 6.3 million people could lose benefits in the proposed rule's first year, with advocates warning of increased hunger risk and added burdens for Alabama administrators.
 Follow Unfollow Recent posts By Wesley Walter Follow Unfollow Recent posts Wesley Walter is a reporter. You can reach him at [email protected] . Published November 17, 2026 Read online: https://www.alreporter.com/2026/11/17/alabama-arise-raises-alarm-regarding-proposal-to-limit-snap-eligibility
 Listen Share Share article

 Nonprofit Alabama Arise has condemned a supplemental nutrition rule change proposed by the U.S. Department of Agriculture that could eliminate millions of people's access to benefits.
 The nonprofit, which works on behalf of Alabamians who live in poverty, has described the USDA’s proposal to end broad-based categorical eligibility, or BBCE, for the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP, as putting Alabamians facing hunger at further risk, while placing new administrative burdens on state SNAP administrators as they are fighting to keep payment error rates in check.
 BBCE is a practice which allows states to raise SNAP income limits to more than 130 percent of the federal poverty level and limit asset tests for individuals who qualify for other federal assistance programs such as Temporary Assistance for Needy Families, or TANF.
 Advertisement
 Current SNAP regulations allow BBCE for families in which all individuals receive TANF benefits, including cash benefits as well as non-cash or in-kind benefits or services from TANF-funded programs.
 The proposed rule would mandate that states may only allow categorical eligibility for families in which each household member receives cash assistance from TANF.

 Copy instruction Open ChatGPT (opens in a new tab) The USDA has argued the change would save the federal government roughly $45 billion over the next five years.
 However, the department has also estimated that the proposed change would prompt 17.6 percent of SNAP beneficiaries, or 6.3 million individuals, to lose access to the program within the rule’s first year in effect.
 Arise Hunger Policy Advocate LaTrell Clifford Wood told APR that the proposed rule would have “massive implications for people who are most adversely impacted by hunger.”
 Advertisement
 The Arise advocate said the proposal follows substantial shifts in SNAP eligibility requirements and funding procedures brought by last year’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act.
 The OBBBA enacted work reporting requirements for individuals previously exempt, including veterans, houseless individuals, those recently aged out of foster care and many individuals with disabilities.
 “The implications of [the proposal] in Alabama are jarring because we have already, in the past year, since the passage of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, seen over 90,000 people essentially purged from these programs, many of whom are eligible for SNAP, but just cannot jump over these eligibility hurdles,” Clifford Wood said.
 Clifford Wood described BBCE as allowing families with moderate savings to still be eligible for benefits in times of need.
 Alongside higher income thresholds, BBCE allows SNAP eligibility without asset limits. Alabama applies standard federal asset limits to SNAP beneficiaries without BBCE, of $3,000 in countable resources per household or $4,500 for applicants who are elderly or disabled.
 Advertisement
 “In those households, particularly with children, it means that those children could lose access to no-cost school meals because SNAP is a means by which they are made automatically eligible for those programs,” Clifford Wood said.
 The OBBBA’s work reporting requirements came alongside new SNAP cost-sharing requirements, mandating that states with an error rate of more than 6 percent must begin taking on responsibility for a portion of SNAP’s operating costs, beginning October of next year.
 Arise and organizations opposed to the proposal have argued the rule would burden county SNAP administrators to administer additional asset tests and eligibility verifications, risking an uptick in the state’s error rate.
 “This rule, specifically, will not bode over well with payment error rates as it serves the potential to increase errors in payments,” Clifford Wood said. “Our DHR agents will now have to go to greater lengths to essentially verify whether or not a household has assets and how much those assets are worth.”
 “The more things that the DHR has to verify—that increases the chances of both under- and overpayments,” the Arise hunger advocate added.
 Advertisement
 Alabama’s SNAP error rate as of late October is 7.89 percent, down from 9.25 percent in 2025.
 The 2025 error rate would have meant that the state would be required to pay 10 percent of SNAP costs or roughly $174 million annually when cost-sharing requirements take effect next year.
 If the state’s error rate remains below 8 percent, Alabama will be required to provide 5 percent of SNAP’s administrative costs when the requirements take effect next year, marking around $90 million in savings per year compared to the 10 percent rate.
 If the state lowers error rates to below 6 percent, it would not have to pay any additional SNAP costs.
 However, states with error rates greater than 13.34 percent in the 2025 and 2026 fiscal years will receive a temporary exemption from cost sharing until the 2030 fiscal year.
 Advertisement
 The USDA is holding a public comment period on its BBCE proposal, which will run until December 10.
 “This is an extremely truncated comment period,” Clifford Wood said. “It is conveniently happening at the same time in which we have a short window for Congress to pass some sort of vehicle that has a two-year cost shift delay so that our DHR can have the same opportunity as other states that are not performing at the degree that Alabama is performing.”
 The Arise advocate urged Alabamians to contact their congressional representatives and voice opposition to the USDA eligibility proposal and call for a pause to upcoming cost-sharing requirements.
